newsitem.title: JAPAN: Scandal-hit DKB says cuts ties with racketeers.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-hit DKB says cuts ties with racketeers.

text.p: Japan's scandal-tainted Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank insisted on Friday that it had cut its ties with the underworld and promised shareholders it will keep its hands clean.
"The new management will completely reject any requests from racketeers," managing director Katsuyuki Sugita told the bank's annual shareholders' meeting.
Sugita's appointment as president of DKB, one of Japan's biggest banks, took effect after the meeting.
Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, along with Nomura Securities Co Ltd, is embroiled in a high-profile scandal over payoffs to "sokaiya" racketeers. The affair has already led to more than a dozen arrests.
The scandal has tainted the image of Japan's financial sector just as Tokyo kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms aimed at introducing more competition into the long-protected sector.

Nomura President Junichi Ujiie, who assumed his post in May after a sweeping management shake-up sparked by the scandal, meanwhile, told the brokerage's shareholders that executives would seek to cut off ties with sokaiya.
"We as executives will endeavour to firmly cut ties with anti-social elements such as sokaiya," Ujiie said.
DKB's Sugita apologised to shareholders for causing them trouble because of the scandal, but acknowledged that the bank still had 7.5 billion yen ($65.7 million) of loans outstanding to racketeers.
Japan's Commercial Code has since 1983 banned payoffs to sokaiya, who extort money from firms by threatening to disrupt shareholders' meetings or disclose dubious management activities.

Many firms, however, have found it tough to end the relationships. On Friday more than 2,300 companies held their meetings in a traditional effort to foil sokaiya by bunching the gatherings on the same day.
DKB earlier this month announced a massive management shake-up, including Sugita's selection as president and the resignation of 21 of its 40 directors to improve its image.

The bank was forced to scrap an initial plan to promote vice president Ichiro Fujita to the presidency due to his alleged role in the sokaiya scandal, and Fujita was arrested on June 13 on suspicion of making illegal loans.
On Thursday, prosecutors indicted four former executives of DKB on charges of making loans totalling 11.78 billion yen ($103 million) to racketeer Ryuichi Koike, the central figure in the scandal.
They were the first DKB executives to be indicted.

A record 855 shareholders turned out for Nomura's gathering on Friday, topping the previous record of 542 who attended Nomura's annual meeting in 1991. That was when the brokerage was entangled in another huge scandal over links to gangsters and improper compensation to favoured clients.

Prosecutors last week charged Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki with illegal payoffs totalling 49.73 million yen ($436,000) to Koike and served him with a fresh arrest warrant on suspicion of paying him another 320 million yen ($2.80 million) on a separate occasion.

Nomura said on Friday that it would consider filing a damages suit against Sakamaki, who stepped down in March when the scandal broke, as well as against two other former executives accused of conspiring with him over the payoffs.
The brokerage itself has been formally charged with breaking the law in connection with the scandal.
Some 10,000 police were mobilised on Friday to help firms cope with the sokaiya threat, Japanese media said.
"Sokaiya, desperate for their survival, have tried to keep their underground ties with firms," said Fumio Serigawa, head of Metropolitan Police Department's anti-gangster section.

"Firms, prompted by the DKB and Nomura case, are trying to cut ties with sokaiya and that means there is mounting tension between them," Serigawa said. The number of sokaiya has declined since payoffs were banned, but police believe there are still about 1,000 racketeers still active.

Stung by criticism that their secretive management ways leave them prey to sokaiya and that they disregard legitimate shareholders' interests, some firms -- including DKB -- let reporters watch the meetings on TV monitors. Nomura made an account of the proceedings available on the Internet.
